overview_audit.lens: Does the evidence under the Overview actually hold it up? I re-derived every figure in 'The list has two clocks, and one of them stopped' from the cluster records it is computed from (scripts/build.py lines 255-277; scripts/clusters.py), checked the nine-item chronology for dates and framing, and checked the Knodel closing paragraph against our own ARG-A07 record (scripts/_b8_A07.py). Headline: the numbers are arithmetically correct and the sentences around them claim things the numbers do not support. The 'all but one' post-1950 result is an artifact of a first-year regex match over a field that mixes what the list cites with what refutes it; the 'no new experiment in ninety years' conclusion rests on a chronology in which the tradition produced none of the nine experiments; and the Knodel paragraph asserts in our own voice what ARG-A07 explicitly refuses to lean on, sourced from two press transcriptions with no timecoded viewing of the film.
overview_audit.strongest_paragraph: 'And part of what this reacts to actually happened... the mediocrity principle is a methodological rule... heliocentrism does not refute human significance. It declines to adjudicate it.' (Why empty proofs keep working, third paragraph.) It concedes something real before answering it, the distinction is exact, and it asks no dataset to carry it.
overview_audit.weakest_paragraph: 'With one exception, and it is the most interesting item on this page. In 2018 Bob Knodel bought a laser ring gyroscope...' (closing paragraph of The list has two clocks). Every load-bearing phrase - 'competently run', 'on camera', 'his own apparatus', '360 divided by 24', 'one exception' - is either unsupported by, or explicitly disclaimed in, our own ARG-A07 treatment.

findings.quote: In 2018 Bob Knodel bought a laser ring gyroscope and used it to test whether the Earth rotates — a real experiment, competently run, exactly what the method asks for.
findings.problem: 'Competently run' is asserted in our own voice about an experiment nobody on this project has watched. ARG-A07 says the opposite three times: the locator - 'Transcribed here from two press accounts of the film ... No timecoded viewing of the film was made for this entry and the surrounding edit was not verified'; the gloss - 'No make, model, input-axis orientation or uncertainty is given in the sequences the press transcriptions cover, so the reading is treated throughout as reported speech and never as a measurement this page relies on'; the refutation - it arrives 'with no make, no model, no input-axis orientation, no uncertainty, no duration and no repeat, and it is not evidence this page leans on.' A reading with none of those stated is exactly what cannot be called competently run, and the Overview leans the section's punchline on it. The treatment's own word is 'The design was sound' - a claim about design, which is defensible; 'competently run' is a claim about execution, which is not.
findings.fix: Match the treatment: 'a sound experimental design - the right instrument, the right quantity, an unambiguous prediction.' Drop 'competently run' unless someone watches the sequence with a timecode and records make, orientation and duration.

findings.quote: Of the ten arguments whose cited work postdates 1950, nine are misappropriated astronomy — microwave-background maps, quasar surveys, the Pioneer anomaly, the Hubble tension.
findings.problem: The 'ten' is not the set of arguments whose cited work postdates 1950. build.py dates each cluster by the FIRST four-digit year in real_source (_YR.search, line 262), so an argument is dated by whatever it cites first. A12's real_source is 'Miller 1933, Rev. Mod. Phys. 5:203; Shankland et al. 1955, Rev. Mod. Phys. 27:167' - it cites 1955 work and is excluded. Recomputed on the latest year in each string, the set is eleven and the non-lane-E members are A12 and R12: nine of eleven, not all-but-one. Three further arguments cite post-1950 work carrying no digits, invisible to the regex entirely - A05 ('ESA Gaia DR3', 2022), R05 ('Gravity Probe B') and A07 ('standard ring-laser INS engineering') - and all three are lane A, not E. On the widest consistent reading it is nine of fourteen, five exceptions. The 'all but one' shape survives none of these readings.
findings.fix: Change the derivation to max(years) and publish the honest ratio, or narrow the words to what is computed ('whose earliest cited work postdates 1950'). The first is better; the second is a strange quantity to publish.

findings.quote: A tradition that describes itself as evidence-led has not produced a new experiment in about ninety years.
findings.problem: The chronology above does not support this, because the tradition produced none of the nine experiments in it - Bradley, Coriolis, Bessel, Foucault, Airy, Michelson, Morley, Sagnac, Gale and Miller were all outsiders to the movement. The bridge sentence concedes it ('the list of things anybody in this tradition points to as an experiment' - points to, not produced), and the next paragraph silently converts citation into production, dating the drought from a 1933 paper by a mainstream physicist at Case. The tradition's own experiment is in our dataset and absent from the chronology: B03, 'Bedford Level / laser canal tests show no curvature', originator Samuel Rowbotham, 1838, whose real_source is 'Wallace 1870; Oldham 1901' - the two reruns that refuted it. Measured against experiments the movement actually produced, the interval neither is ninety years nor starts in 1933.
findings.fix: Publish the stronger, better-supported finding: the tradition's experimental authorities are all borrowed, and it has produced almost no experiments of its own at any point - Rowbotham's canal trials in 1838, then a very long gap.

findings.quote: It is not an experiment about whether the Earth moves, and none of it was designed to be one.
findings.problem: 'None of it' is refuted by our own records for two of the arguments being counted. E03's note reads 'The dipole *is* our motion - 369.82 +/- 0.11 km/s, measured', and its real_source is Kashlinsky 2008 and Planck Int. XIII 2014 - bulk-flow work whose purpose is to measure the observer's velocity, i.e. a measurement of whether and how fast the Earth moves. And the eleventh argument the sentence quietly excludes, R12, cites Zhang and Stebbins 2011, of which our note says 'It is not merely assumed - it is tested. The kSZ power spectrum rules out Gpc-scale off-centre void models' - a purpose-built test of whether we occupy a special location. This is also the unscoped-absence failure in new dress: a claim about the design intent of a whole literature, made from a nine-row sample.
findings.fix: Scope it - 'most of it was gathered to characterise the universe, not to test the Earth's motion' - and keep the exception visible, since the CMB dipole being a direct measurement of our motion argues this page's case better than the blanket does.

findings.quote: With one exception, and it is the most interesting item on this page.
findings.problem: The same tab says two, three paragraphs later: 'That moment is on film, twice, from the same community, with opposite outcomes.' The second filmed experiment - the light-through-three-holes test closing Behind the Curve - is named in the very Newsweek source ARG-A07 cites ('transcription of the gyroscope quote and the closing light experiment'). Beyond the film there is a counter-example the page does not mention: The Final Experiment, Union Glacier, Antarctica, 14-17 December 2024 - eight participants, four of them flat-earth proponents, three days of livestreamed midnight sun, after which Jeran Campanella said on camera that his model was no longer valid. A defender names that in one line and both 'one exception' and 'about ninety years' fall.
findings.fix: Reconcile the two sections and add the 2024 expedition. It is better evidence for this review's thesis than Knodel: the concession is unambiguous and on the record, and part of the community rejected the footage as faked - the exact moment the page says it is looking for.

findings.quote: After 1950 the citations change character entirely.
findings.problem: The change of character is our own taxonomy read back to us, not something measured. 'Misappropriated astronomy' is the name of lane E (LANE_NAME['E'] = 'E - Misappropriated astronomy', build.py line 28) and the count behind the following sentence is literally CLUSTERS[c]['lane'] != 'E' (line 277). Seven of the nine (E02, E04, E05, E06, E08, E09, E12) have no treatment at all - 14 of 18 lane-E arguments sit at cluster depth - so the classification carrying the section's central claim is the part of the dataset no reviewer has attacked.
findings.fix: Name the mechanism in the following sentence ('nine of them sit in the misappropriated-astronomy family') so the reader knows it is our taxonomy, and say how many of the nine are still at cluster depth. The Under-construction module above already sets that precedent.

findings.quote: Sorted by the real work each argument points at, the specimen does not look like a modern document.
findings.problem: real_source does not hold only the work the argument points at; for a substantial minority it holds the work that refutes it, mixed into the same string. B03: 'Wallace 1870; Oldham 1901' (the reruns that refuted Rowbotham). E12: 'Tifft 1976; refuted by 2dF/SDSS surveys'. E08: Turyshev 2012 is the resolution of the Pioneer anomaly. E05: Patel and Desmond 2024 is the isotropy result. A12: Shankland 1955 is the demolition of Miller. E06 is the clean case - its only real_source is 'Sawala et al. 2023, Nature Astronomy 7:481', the paper showing the satellite plane is transient, while its three items are 'Cluster axes ecliptic', 'Dwarf galaxy planes coherence', 'Satellite alignments'. E06 therefore enters the post-1950 nine on the strength of a citation to its own refutation. Every figure in the section - 28, 115, 1933, 61, ten, nine - comes from that mixed field.
findings.fix: Split real_source into cited_work and counter_source, or narrow the sentence to what the field is: 'sorted by the dated work each argument is anchored to, theirs and ours'. The split is the right fix; the counts would then mean what the sentence says.

findings.quote: Twenty-eight arguments cite a dated piece of genuine science between them, covering 115 items, and the median year of that work is 1933.
findings.problem: Two faults in one sentence. (1) 'genuine science': the earliest of the 28, which anchors the distribution, is C07 - 'Robert Bellarmine to Paolo Antonio Foscarini, 12 April 1615', a cardinal's letter on scriptural interpretation. D04 ('Eliade 1949; Guenon, Le Roi du Monde 1927') and D05 (Eliade, Patterns in Comparative Religion) are history of religions. Three of the 28 are not science on any reading. (2) The median: 1933 is the 15th of 28 unweighted cluster years; the median of 28 values is 1931. Placing it immediately after 'covering 115 items' invites the item-weighted reading, which gives 1925 - the 58th of 115 items falls in the Michelson-Gale bucket, not Miller's.
findings.fix: 'Twenty-eight arguments are anchored to a dated publication', and state which median: 'the median argument's source year is 1933; weighted by items it is 1925.' Both numbers help the case.

findings.quote: The experiments run in a straight line and then stop: Bradley on aberration in 1729, Coriolis in 1835, Bessel measuring the first stellar parallax in 1838, Foucault's pendulum in 1851, Airy's water-filled telescope in 1871, Michelson and Morley in 1887, Sagnac in 1913, Michelson–Gale in 1925, and Miller's aether drift in 1933
findings.problem: Three of the nine are not experiments. Coriolis 1835 (Sur les equations du mouvement relatif des systemes de corps) is a theoretical mechanics paper; Coriolis ran no experiment. Bradley 1729 and Bessel 1838 are observations. The closing clause 'That is the list of things anybody in this tradition points to as an experiment' does not repair the opening 'The experiments run in a straight line.' The dates also mix experiment with publication: our own ARG-A03 steelman says Airy 'mounted it in 1870, observed gamma Draconis for two years' - 1871 is the paper - and Miller's observations ran 1921-26, with 1933 the Rev. Mod. Phys. summary. The ninety-year interval is measured off that publication date.
findings.fix: 'The results run in a straight line and then stop' fixes the category error in one word. If 'experiments' stays, drop Coriolis or relabel him: 'Coriolis's rotating-frame equations, 1835'.

findings.quote: It returned 15 degrees per hour. That is 360 divided by 24.
findings.problem: Wrong quantity, and our own treatment says so. A ring laser senses rotation with respect to the local inertial frame, so the rate a rotating Earth predicts is the sidereal 15.041 deg/hr = 360/23.934, not 360/24 = 15.000. A07's gloss states both figures and then declines the inference: 'the figure as spoken carries two significant figures and cannot separate them, so nothing here claims that this apparatus resolved sidereal from solar.' The Overview publishes the two-significant-figure coincidence as the identification. The companion clause 'It is the answer the globe predicts' compounds it: A07 says 'a single-axis unit with its input axis vertical reads only Omega sin phi' (about 9.7 deg/hr at 40 N) and 'Nothing in this treatment depends on which it was' - but the Overview's claim does depend on it.
findings.fix: 'He reported 15 degrees per hour - the rate a rotating Earth predicts, to the two significant figures the statement carries.'

findings.quote: obtained by a flat-earth researcher using his own apparatus, on camera
findings.problem: Two unsupported words. 'On camera' attaches to 'obtained', implying the measurement was filmed; what the footage carries is Knodel describing a result afterwards, and per A07 nobody on this project has viewed the sequence at all. 'His own' asserts ownership the record does not establish - the press accounts A07 cites describe a group purchase, and A07 deliberately withholds the cost line ('the only use for it is to invite a reader to infer a motive') to stay out of that territory; 'his own' walks back into it without the evidence.
findings.fix: 'reported on camera by a flat-earth researcher, using apparatus the group had bought for the purpose.'

findings.quote: Bessel measuring the first stellar parallax in 1838
findings.problem: Priority is contested and the page states it flat. Struve published a preliminary Vega parallax in 1837; Henderson observed Alpha Centauri in 1832-33 and published in January 1839. Bessel's claim is to the first reliably published measurement, which is how it is normally phrased. The project's own build.py guard forbids this word in the analogous case - 'say EARLIEST DOCUMENTED, never first - we cannot show anything is first' (lines 119-120) - and our own A05 real_source records the fact without it: 'Bessel 1838 (61 Cygni, 0.314 arcsec)'.
findings.fix: 'Bessel publishing the first reliable stellar parallax in 1838.' One word, and it removes a free hit for anyone who knows the Struve/Henderson story.

findings.quote: which Michelson, Pease and Pearson had already contradicted in 1929 and Shankland took apart in 1955
findings.problem: 'Already' is true only against Miller's 1933 summary paper, not against the work. Miller's Mount Wilson observations ran 1921-26, before the 1929 null, so the sentence reads as though he published a result that had been refuted in advance. Our own A12 note frames the refutation on a different and stronger axis - 'Shankland et al. re-examined Miller's original data sheets and traced the periodic shifts to reading statistics and local temperature variation. Shankland had been Miller's own student and colleague' - and does not rely on the ordering.
findings.fix: '...whose observations ran 1921-26, and which Michelson, Pease and Pearson's null contradicted in 1929 before Shankland took it apart in 1955.'

overview_audit.lens: Fairness, tone and overclaim on the Overview tab (scripts/render.py `tab_overview`, lines 405-585, plus the masthead in `BODY` at lines 812-818, as rendered in docs/index.html). Two full adversarial sweeps have covered 35 argument treatments and none of this text. The dominant pattern: every number is correctly derived in scripts/build.py, and the sentences wrapped around those numbers repeatedly claim something the derivation cannot see. The second pattern is worse for this project specifically — the front page commits, in bold, the exact failures the argument treatments are written to avoid. ARG-A07's published gloss says "This page makes no claim about why"; the Overview section directly above it is titled "Why empty proofs keep working" and answers why. ARG-A07 says the gyroscope reading "is treated throughout as reported speech and never as a measurement this page relies on"; the Overview relies on it and calls it the most interesting item on the page. The hedge rule is enforced downward onto 35 treatments and nowhere applied to the 900 words most readers actually read.
overview_audit.strongest_paragraph: "And part of what this reacts to actually happened. Popular science does deploy cosmic scale as an argument about meaning — the mote-of-dust register is a staple. But the mediocrity principle is a methodological rule... So, plainly: heliocentrism does not refute human significance. It declines to adjudicate it." This is the only place in the Overview that concedes ground on the other side's terms, names a real thing the other side is responding to, and makes a distinction that costs the page something. It is also the only paragraph whose central claim is about ideas rather than about people's insides. If the whole "Why empty proofs keep working" section were rebuilt to this paragraph's standard, most of the findings below would disappear.
overview_audit.weakest_paragraph: "If the 98 arguments do not discriminate — and none of them does — a question follows that the evidence review cannot answer on its own: why does any of this persist? The genealogy suggests the answer. Belief here was never sustained by the evidence, so removing the evidence does not touch it." Three sentences, and the paragraph itself concedes that the evidence review cannot answer the question — then answers it anyway, from a genealogy of texts, about the mental states of living people, in the past absolute ("was never"). It is the form of claim the page's own legend calls UNFALSIFIABLE, deployed as the thesis of the section. Everything after it inherits the problem.

findings.quote: Belief here was never sustained by the evidence, so removing the evidence does not touch it.
findings.problem: This attributes a mental state to a community of mostly living people, in the past absolute, on the basis of a genealogy of texts. Text provenance can establish who wrote what and when; it cannot establish what sustains anyone's belief. The sentence before it concedes exactly this ("a question ... that the evidence review cannot answer on its own") and then it is answered anyway. It is also unfalsifiable by construction — no observation could disconfirm it — which is the category the page's own legend defines as "outside testable measurement" and applies to others. Worst, it is flatly contradicted by the project's most carefully written treatment: ARG-A07's gloss publishes "Bob Knodel is living, and everything below treats these words as an honest description of what an apparatus displayed and what was done next. This page makes no claim about why." The Overview section is titled "Why empty proofs keep working."
findings.fix: Replace the motive claim with the behaviour claim the dataset actually supports: that the arguments do not discriminate, that the citations stopped being experiments after the 1930s, and that on the two filmed occasions where a prediction was tested the outcome did not settle the question. Say what was observed, not what sustains it. If the section must speculate, mark it as speculation in its own voice ("we do not know why, and this review has no instrument for it") rather than as a finding the genealogy delivered.

findings.quote:
A provenance review of the flat-earth
     & geocentric “proof” lists — tracing 461 claims back to
     19 authors.
findings.problem: Untrue as written, and it is the site's one-sentence self-description, rendered above the tab bar so it sits on every tab. 348 of the 461 items trace to the 19 named people; 113 have no named originator and 32 clusters are untraced. The Overview's own lead paragraph two inches below gets it right ("348 of them trace to 19 named people"), which makes this a compression of our own accurate sentence that drops the qualifier — the drift_type the project calls hedge_dropped, in the masthead. "lists" plural also generalises a review of one specimen to a genre.
findings.fix: "tracing 348 of 461 claims back to 19 authors" — or "tracing a 461-item list back to 19 authors and 31 dead ends". Fix the plural too: one list was reviewed.

findings.quote: Twenty-eight arguments cite a dated piece of genuine science between them, covering 115 items, and the median year of that work is 1933.
findings.problem: The figure is derived; the words are not. build.py's `_dated` list is built by regex-matching the first four-digit year in each cluster's `real_source_cited` field — it makes no judgement about whether the cited work is science. Three of the 28 are not: C07 is "Robert Bellarmine to Paolo Antonio Foscarini, 12 April 1615" (a theological letter, 9 items), D04 is "Eliade 1949; Guénon, Le Roi du Monde 1927" (6 items) and D05 is Eliade's Patterns in Comparative Religion (2 items). That is 17 of the 115 items. "genuine science" is doing the paragraph's rhetorical work — the whole section is about experiments — and it is false for three of the twenty-eight.
findings.fix: "Twenty-eight arguments cite a dated work between them" — or exclude the non-science clusters from the derivation in build.py and republish the smaller figure. Do not let a regex over a free-text field license the adjective.

findings.quote: Most of those items rest on something published before 1930: 61 of 115.
findings.problem: This is the branch of a self-selecting sentence whose comment in render.py explains it picks its form from the arithmetic so the page cannot say "most" of a minority. The safeguard is defeated by the previous finding: 9 of the 61 pre-1930 items are C07, Bellarmine's 1615 letter. Remove the one item in the bucket that is unambiguously not science and it becomes 52 of 106 — at which point 52*2 = 104 < 106 and the sentence's own else-branch fires, rendering "52 of those 106 items rest on something published before 1930" with no "Most". The claim survives only because a theological letter is being counted as science.
findings.fix: Same fix as above; the branch logic is sound and should be fed a bucket that matches the words. Note in the test suite that the majority is currently 53% and one cluster reclassification flips it.

findings.quote: A tradition that describes itself as evidence-led has not produced a new experiment in about ninety years.
findings.problem: The derivation cannot support this. `_dated` reads the dates of the mainstream works each argument points at — it is structurally blind to experiments the movement ran, because such an experiment only enters the dataset when it happens to be somebody's `real_source_cited`. Absence of a post-1933 date in that field is not absence of an experiment. And the page supplies its own counterexample in the next paragraph: Knodel's 2018 gyroscope test, which this same Overview calls "a real experiment, competently run". The gap is eight years, not ninety. "With one exception" opening the following paragraph does not repair a bolded sentence that states a universal — this is precisely the compression the project objects to when a list item does it, committed in bold on the front page.
findings.fix: "The specimen cites no experiment performed after 1933 — with one exception, and it is the most interesting item on this page." That is what the dataset shows, it scopes to the specimen, and it makes the Knodel paragraph the payoff instead of a contradiction.

findings.quote: That is the list of things anybody in this tradition points to as an experiment.
findings.problem: An absence asserted about a living, worldwide community from a single 461-item specimen — the failure mode curmudgeon.md names as "the dominant failure — nine confirmed", and the exact construction the house rule bans. The rule requires "X is not located in <the text you searched>"; the text searched here is one list retrieved on 2026-08-02. The sentence instead quantifies over "anybody in this tradition". The prose-lint regex does not scan render.py's BODY, which is presumably why it is still here — curmudgeon.md's own verdict applies: "writers have learned the regex, not the rule."
findings.fix: "That is every experiment the specimen points at." Then extend the absence-claim test to the render.py Overview strings, since a green ratchet is evidence only about the fields it reads.

findings.quote: It returned 15 degrees per hour. That is 360 divided by 24. It is the answer the globe predicts, obtained by a flat-earth researcher using his own apparatus, on camera.
findings.problem: Every hedge carried by ARG-A07 is stripped here, on a named living private individual. The treatment's own locator says the quote is "Transcribed here from two press accounts of the film ... which differ in small ways. No timecoded viewing of the film was made for this entry and the surrounding edit was not verified." Its gloss says "the reading is treated throughout as reported speech and never as a measurement this page relies on", that no make, model, input-axis orientation or uncertainty is known, and that "nothing here claims that this apparatus resolved sidereal from solar" — because 15 to two significant figures cannot separate 15.000 from the sidereal 15.041. The Overview states the reading as a measurement, states it is "the answer the globe predicts", and calls the whole thing "the most interesting item on this page" — i.e. relies on it maximally. "competently run" is also stronger than the treatment's finding, which locates the fault in a protocol with no stated acceptance criterion.
findings.fix: Carry one clause of the treatment's hedging into the front page: "On camera, by his own account, it read 15 degrees per hour — the rate a rotating Earth predicts and the rate a stationary one puts at zero. See ARG-A07 for what the sourcing of that quote will and will not carry." If the front page cannot afford the hedge, it cannot afford the example.

findings.quote: That moment is on film, twice, from the same community, with opposite outcomes.
findings.problem: A claim about two identifiable people's belief-updating, unsourced, on the closing line of a section, on a page whose entire subject is provenance. One instance is presumably ARG-A07, linked six paragraphs earlier; the second is named nowhere and linked nowhere, so a reader cannot check it and a critic can pick whichever pair is most convenient. And ARG-A07 itself refuses the inference this sentence draws from it: "inferring motive from a filmed remark is the move this review exists to object to when it is done to us." The sentence is generous in structure — "opposite outcomes" concedes that one person did update — which makes it more frustrating that it is undocumented.
findings.fix: Name and link both, with dates, or cut the sentence. If the second instance is a public retraction by a named person, it is the single best thing in this section and deserves its own treatment rather than a trailing clause.

findings.quote: One is about who gets to be believed. The other is about whether we are incidental.
findings.problem: The paragraph hedges once — "they appear to run on different needs" — and then spends the hedge immediately, stating the two lineages' motives flatly in two consecutive declaratives. This is drift_type hedge_dropped occurring inside a single paragraph of our own prose. What is observable is what the texts argue about: the zetetic texts argue about method and authority, the Tychonian texts argue theologically. What people's beliefs are "about", in the sense of what need they serve, is not observable from a corpus.
findings.fix: Keep the hedge live across both sentences: "One reads as an argument about who gets to be believed; the other as an argument about whether we are incidental." That describes the texts, which is what was read.

findings.quote: All 461 items are assigned to an argument, a source family and a verdict, derived from the dataset rather than asserted. The scorecard and the family counts are final.
findings.problem: Two problems in one row of the falsifiability module. First, "derived from the dataset rather than asserted" is circular: the assignments and verdicts are hand-authored in clusters.py and assign.py and *are* the assertion; build.py derives counts from them. Presenting editorial judgement as measurement is the strongest claim on a module whose whole purpose is honesty about what is unfinished. Second, "final" is contradicted by the project's own published limit on the Method tab — "Cluster boundaries involve judgement. A handful of items could sit in an adjacent argument; that would move counts by a few units" — and family counts are a direct function of cluster assignment, so they move when items move.
findings.fix: "All 461 items are assigned to an argument, a source family and a verdict, and every count on this page is computed from those assignments rather than estimated. The assignments themselves involve judgement — see Known limits." Drop "final".

findings.quote: Attributions independently audited
findings.problem: Nothing about this is independent — the audits are performed by the same project, in the same repository, and the row's own number is `S["arguments_at_full_depth"]`, the identical figure used by the row above for "Arguments written in full". So "33/98 audited" is "33/98 written up" relabelled; the module publishes the same measurement twice under two different claims. It also reads as 33 attributions that passed, when the Method tab reports that 13 of those 33 turned up an error in our own record. "Roughly a third of spot-checks failing" is the honest headline and it is two tabs away.
findings.fix: Drop "independently". Retitle the row "Attributions re-checked against the primary text" and put the failure rate in the status sub-label — "33/98 checked, 13 found faulty" — which is more damaging and much more credible than the current badge.

findings.quote: This page is being built in the open. The scorecard above is complete; the prose beneath it is not. Nothing here is hidden behind a progress bar.
findings.problem: The claim of full disclosure is not honoured. The README's fourth known limit — "The corpus was extracted via an intermediary model. Two independent fetches agreed character-for-character on a spot-checked range, but re-verify any single item against the live page before making its exact wording load-bearing" — appears nowhere in docs/index.html. The word "intermediary" occurs exactly once in the rendered page and it is about rivers flowing in intermediary directions. The Method tab's Known limits list carries four bullets (untraced items, the soft author count, cluster boundaries, Carpenter 1885) and omits it. Every count on the page rests on that extraction, and a module that says nothing is hidden is the wrong place to omit it.
findings.fix: Add the extraction caveat as a fifth Known-limits bullet and, given that it conditions the 461 itself, a clause in the module: "The specimen text was captured via an intermediary model and spot-checked, not re-keyed."

findings.quote: Why empty proofs keep working
findings.problem: "Empty" contradicts the page's own findings and its own steelmanning standard. By the verdict distribution rendered 400 pixels below this heading, 90 items are STANDARD PHYSICS — defined in the legend as "real, already explained, does not discriminate" — and 88 are MISLEADING, "real data, wrong conclusion". ARG-A07's steelman says in terms: "The argument identifies the correct instrument, the correct physical quantity and a prediction the two models disagree about by the whole of it." None of that is empty. The finding is that the items do not discriminate, which is a much more interesting claim and the one the page spent 461 items earning.
findings.fix: "Why non-discriminating proofs keep working", or "Why the list keeps working anyway". The heading should name the finding, not editorialise past it.

findings.quote: Someone who bristles at the slide from the first to the second is responding to something that was genuinely said.
findings.problem: This is the section's steelman, and it steelmans a feeling nobody in the corpus is quoted having, rather than any of the 98 arguments. The move imputes a motive — discomfort at cosmic insignificance — and then generously concedes the imputed motive, which reads as fairness while conceding nothing the other side actually argued. Not one of the 19 named people is quoted here. "bristles" also does work: it frames the interlocutor as reacting emotionally rather than reasoning, in a section that is otherwise arguing they are not reasoning from evidence.
findings.fix: Steelman a text. Bouw conceded observational equivalence, and the page knows it (People tab: "Conceded observational equivalence"); Sungenis argues from general covariance and R01/R06 answer it at length. Quoting one of them here would make the section's fairness real instead of performed. At minimum replace "bristles at" with "objects to".

findings.quote: They found the same enemy from opposite directions, which is why the list welds “flat” to “not rotating” even though every Tychonian authority it cites held the Earth to be a sphere.
findings.problem: Two things. "enemy" is loaded — the page has no evidence about what anyone regarded as an enemy, only that both lineages oppose the same body of results; the word converts an observable overlap into an imputed hostility. And "every Tychonian authority it cites held the Earth to be a sphere" is a universal quantifier with no derived support: the dataset carries four Tychonian people and no sphere/flat field on any record, so the claim is an unaudited assertion sitting inside the sentence that carries the section's structural point.
findings.fix: "They converge on the same target from opposite directions." For the second half, either add a field to people.py that records the position and derive the claim, or scope it: "every Tychonian authority the specimen cites whose position we checked".

findings.quote: The zetetic line starts with Rowbotham in 1849, in a secular Owenite commune, and its founding move is epistemic
findings.problem: Contradicted by the project's own People tab, which says "Rowbotham began at Manea Fen, a short-lived Owenite socialist commune in the Cambridgeshire Fens, in the late 1830s." The 1849 pamphlet was not written in the commune — the community was defunct years before. The detail is load-bearing, not decorative: the secular-commune setting is what carries the secular/theological contrast against van der Kamp in the next sentence, so a reader who checks the date finds the contrast resting on a wrong one.
findings.fix: "The zetetic line starts with Rowbotham, whose method was formed in a secular Owenite commune in the late 1830s and first published in 1849." Same contrast, correct chronology, and it matches the People tab.

findings.quote: What it has produced is a growing apparatus for reading other people’s results — which is the opposite of the zetetic method it was founded on, and a thing Rowbotham would have recognised as exactly what he was arguing against.
findings.problem: "A tradition ... the zetetic method it was founded on" fuses the two lineages that this same section insists were "never reconciled with each other" and that the whole page treats as separately originated. The Tychonian line was not founded on the zetetic method; van der Kamp's line is theological from the first page, as the paragraph above says. The post-1950 citation shift the sentence is explaining is overwhelmingly lane E and R12 — not the zetetic lane at all — so the reproach is aimed at the wrong lineage by the page's own lane data. The closing clause additionally asserts a counterfactual mental state of a dead author as fact.
findings.fix: Scope it: "which is the opposite of the zetetic method one half of it was founded on". And downgrade the last clause to what is documented — Rowbotham's published definition of zetetic against "theoretic" is quoted on the People tab and makes the point without ventriloquism.

findings.quote: This review sorts one representative specimen by where each claim came from.
findings.problem: "representative" is an unsupported claim doing real work — it is what licenses every generalisation in the Overview from this list to "this tradition". Nothing in the dataset compares this list to any other; no second list was sampled. The README uses the same word with the same absence of support.
findings.fix: "one specimen", and if representativeness matters to the argument, earn it: a paragraph noting the overlap with Dubay's 200 Proofs and Carpenter's format would substantiate it in three sentences.

findings.quote: Unchecked is not a claim that the phrasing is faithful; it means nobody has compared them yet — and a further 2 was traced to no author at all.
findings.problem: Number/verb disagreement, and the noun is missing — "a further 2" of what? Arguments. On a row whose entire purpose is precision about what has and has not been checked, a sentence that cannot say what its own number counts undercuts the row. Elsewhere the page uses the `w()` helper to spell small counts for exactly this reason; this one bypasses it.
findings.fix: f'and a further {w(S["hedge_no_source"])} arguments were traced to no author at all' — with singular/plural handled, since the figure can move to 1.

findings.quote: Twenty-eight arguments cite a dated piece of genuine science between them, covering 115 items, and the median year of that work is 1933.
findings.problem: Secondary to the "genuine science" finding above, and worth separating because it is a different kind of error: the median is computed per argument (build.py takes `_years[len(_years)//2]` over 28 cluster years) but is presented inside a sentence whose subject has just been restated as "115 items". A reader takes 1933 as the median an item points at. Item-weighted, the median falls at 1925 — which is a better number for the paragraph's thesis, so the imprecision is not even self-serving.
findings.fix: Say which median it is — "the median argument cites work from 1933" — or publish the item-weighted figure and label it as such.

findings.problem: The steelman says the solar quadrupole "has since been measured, twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" and then immediately names "ranging to the MESSENGER spacecraft in orbit at Mercury" as the second method - which refutation section 4 itself describes as measuring J2 "from Mercury's own orbit". This is the exact sentence the preemptive designates as the answer to the advocate's circularity objection (rated 3/5), so the load-bearing reply invites the objection it is meant to close. Compounding it, the advocate's charge as drafted is factually wrong about the paper: Park et al. (AJ 153:121, 2017) state they decouple the effects of beta and J2 by taking gamma from the Cassini Shapiro-delay result rather than fitting the PPN parameters and J2 together.
findings.fix: Replace "twice, by methods that do not use Mercury" with "twice, by routes that do not depend on the perihelion residual - one of them without Mercury at all". Then add one sentence to the same paragraph, which is the strongest available answer and is currently absent: Park et al. did not fit J2 against beta and gamma simultaneously - they imported gamma from Cassini and solved for beta and J2 separately, so the degeneracy Dicke identified is broken by data from outside the fit. Correct the advocate's best_defense to charge something the paper actually does, or the preemptive is answering a phantom.

findings.problem: The refutation answers the list's fragment, not the source our own gloss quotes. The gloss locates the argument at Chapter 4 p. 198 (Hoyle: the centre "to be used for any set of bodies depends on the way in which the local system is considered to be isolated from the universe as a whole") and at Chapter 10 p. 598 ("make Earth the immovable barycenter of the universe") - a frame-choice argument about the mass centre of the whole universe, closed with a theological possibility claim ("Certainly no one can object, then, if God had decided long ago to put the Earth in that very barycenter"). Verified verbatim in the OCR. The refutation answers with Sun-Earth versus Sun-Jupiter two-body arithmetic, which is orthogonal to that claim: nothing in the 449 km / 742,900 km comparison bears on where the barycentre of the universe is, and the paragraph never states the conclusion a reader needs (that the solar system's mass centre sits inside or just outside the Sun, 1 AU from the Earth).
findings.fix: Add a paragraph answering the source's version: (a) a barycentre is a coordinate origin, not a dynamically privileged seat - nothing 'rests' there and no observation distinguishes an object at one; (b) what the planetary ephemeris actually fits is relative accelerations, which are unchanged by the choice; (c) the solar-system mass centre is never more than about 2.2 solar radii from the Sun's centre, so on the source's own arithmetic the Earth is not in it; (d) cross-link ARG-R01, where the general-covariance form of Hoyle's point is answered - it is already in `related` but the reader is never routed there. Keep the existing mass-ratio calculation as the answer to item 104's fragment, labelled as such.

findings.field: clusters.py E14 record (originator, originator_work, year, real_source) as rendered against passage/gloss
findings.problem: clusters.py has originator=None and real_source=None for E14, and render.py prints "· no named originator" into the meta line directly above the treatment. The treatment beneath it opens with a Sungenis & Bennett passage, a work record, and four page-located matches in the same volume. On a site whose product is provenance, the summary line next to the verdict chip will contradict the entry a reader has not yet expanded. The entry reports this only in its module docstring, addressed to `record_problems` - a channel with no existence anywhere in this repository (the string appears only inside other batch-9 docstrings; there is no field, file or JSON of that name). This is the batch-8 sweep's pattern C, named there as the highest-leverage defect on the board, recurring.
findings.fix: Owner of clusters.py: anchor on the cluster key "E14", never on the originator= line (byte-identical across B02/B06/B07/D12). Do not set originator="PER-SUNGENIS" - the entry establishes a content match, not a transmission chain, and naming an originator on that evidence is the error the README's three-state rule forbids. Set real_source to the located parallel with the caveat in the note ("four of the five items have a page-located counterpart in Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I; the list carries no citations, so descent is not demonstrated"), and revise the note, which currently addresses only neutrinos and the barycentre and is silent on the two topics in the cluster's own title.

findings.field: sources[1] label (Dicke & Goldenberg) and refutation section 4
findings.problem: The source label reads "the (5.0 +/- 0.7) x 10^-5 figure the source quotes". That is not the figure the source quotes. Sungenis quotes "approximately 40 parts per million" - 4.0 x 10^-5 - which our own passage block reproduces verbatim three fields above, and which the compression source_wording repeats twice ("12 parts per million rather than the original 40"). Refutation section 4 then compares the modern ~8 x 10^-6 values against 5.0 x 10^-5 ("six times larger") rather than against the 4.0 x 10^-5 the source is actually asserting. I confirmed both numbers at source: PRL 18:313 reports (5.0 +/- 0.7) x 10^-5 for the fractional difference of radii, and the OCR reads "approximately 40 parts per million". A defender reading the passage block and then the source list catches the mismatch in one scroll.
findings.fix: Relabel: "Dicke & Goldenberg, 'Solar Oblateness and General Relativity', Phys. Rev. Lett. 18:313 (1967) - the measured (5.0 +/- 0.7) x 10^-5; the source's text renders it as 'approximately 40 parts per million'." In section 4, compare against the source's own 40 ppm ("five times larger") or state both numbers, rather than silently using the larger one.

findings.problem: "the creationist ministry that had promoted the argument put it on a public list of claims to stop using" attributes prior promotion of the neutrino argument to Creation Ministries International. Nothing in the body, the gloss or the sources establishes that. The gloss says only that CMI lists the claim among arguments creationists should not use; the CMI page I checked says creationists should "no longer invoke" it, which is a statement about creationists generally; and the docstring's promoters (Brown 1995, Oard 1995, Davies 1996, Snelling 1997) are named from TalkOrigins with the explicit note that no link to CMI or to this list was established. The TLDR is the field most readers never expand past, and this is a provenance claim on a provenance page - the exact TLDR-stronger-than-body pattern flagged in both prior sweeps.
findings.fix: Replace with: "and the creationist ministry that maintains the standard 'arguments creationists should not use' list retired it publicly." That is exactly what the body and the cited page support, and it loses nothing rhetorically.

findings.field: sources[13] (Fossat et al. 2017) and steelman/refutation treatment of interior rotation
findings.problem: Fossat et al., A&A 604:A40, is in the published source list but is not referenced anywhere in any rendered field - it appears only in the docstring. Meanwhile both the steelman and refutation section 4 assert that helioseismic inversions read the interior rotation "directly" and found the radiative zone "turning close to rigidly", with no mention that the innermost core's rotation is contested. The docstring (section 3d) knows this and knows the answer - Fossat's claimed 3.8x is far short of Dicke's postulated ~20x, and J2 is now measured from an orbit regardless - but the answer never reaches the page. So the entry publishes a citation supporting nothing while omitting the caveat that citation exists to handle, and a defender who has read Fossat gets a free hit on the paragraph that closes Dicke's mechanism.
findings.fix: Add one clause to refutation section 4 after the rigid-rotation sentence: "The innermost core remains contested - Fossat et al. (A&A 604:A40, 2017) inferred 3.8x the envelope rate from asymptotic g modes, a detection others have called fragile - but even that is far short of the roughly twentyfold core Dicke's inference required, and J2 is now measured from a spacecraft orbit rather than inferred from rotation at all." That earns the citation and pre-empts the objection in one sentence.

findings.field: refutation, section 5 ("The step that is left to the reader")
findings.problem: "...is not located in the Vol. I text searched for this entry, whose solar-physics content is the Appendix 5 perihelion argument quoted above." The first half is correctly scoped and the second half quietly un-scopes it: it characterises the whole searched volume as containing one piece of solar-physics content, which is a totalising claim of the shape the absence rule targets, and it sits awkwardly against this entry's own findings - the same volume's Chapter 12 argues about the Sun's motion through the Galaxy at p. 959, Chapter 4 and Chapter 10 argue about the Sun's motion about the barycentre, and the volume discusses a cosmological neutrino sea. It also arrives in the paragraph doing the most rhetorical work ("the source has nothing to offer"), which is where such a sentence costs most. This is the pattern the batch-8 sweep called out as banned constructions migrating into fields the ratchet does not scan.
findings.fix: Cut the appositive and keep the scoped claim: "...is not located in the Vol. I text searched for this entry, whose treatment of the Sun's physical structure is the Appendix 5 perihelion argument quoted above; the volume's other solar material (the apex at p. 959, the barycentre at pp. 198-199 and 598) argues about the Sun's motion, not about what a stationary-Earth model predicts for it."

findings.problem: "Five items, five different situations." The section then enumerates four situations - neutrino deficit, barycentre (104 and 361 together), apex, oblateness - plus a fifth section that is not an item but a meta-observation about the missing inferential step. The TLDR meanwhile opens "Four solar topics bundled as five exhibits", which is the accurate count. The first sentence of the refutation and the first sentence of the TLDR disagree about the entry's own structure.
findings.fix: "Five items, four topics, and four different situations - answered separately, because bundling them is the only thing that makes them look like a pattern."

findings.problem: "Davis spent thirty years on it and was given a Nobel Prize for the anomaly itself." The 2002 physics Nobel citation reads "for pioneering contributions to astrophysics, in particular for the detection of cosmic neutrinos" - it was awarded for the detection, shared with Koshiba and Giacconi, not for the anomaly. The rhetorical point (the field rewarded the person who surfaced the discrepancy) survives a precise wording; the current wording is a checkable overstatement in a field that accuses the source of misrepresentation, which is the worst place to carry one.
findings.fix: "...and Davis spent thirty years on it and shared the 2002 Nobel Prize for the detection that produced the discrepancy."

findings.problem: The published block asserts that "'Interplanetary' returns 22 hits in (B), every one of them either a Maxwell quotation about the aether or a discussion of JPL's probe-navigation equations", and the docstring adds "None about dust." I downloaded the same OCR file (item galileo-was-wrong-the-church-was-right-sungenis-vol-1-3-complete, 5,499,250 bytes) and enumerated all 22. The count is exactly right; the characterisation is not. Several hits are neither category - the 1961 Venus radar contact and the Shapiro/Wallace speed-of-light dispute (4 hits), Galileo's comets in The Assayer, the Mercury perihelion residual, and a general remark about space probes reaching their destinations. One hit is squarely about interplanetary dust: 'a gravitational frequency shift of pioneer signals proportional to distance and the density of the interplanetary dust cannot be responsible for the anomaly; known properties of the dust are not large enough to produce the observed acceleration.' The 'no_source' conclusion is unaffected - nothing in the text argues from zodiacal or Kuiper structure - but this is the one sentence in the entry that a defender can falsify in five minutes with a public download, and it sits in the block whose whole function is to prove the search was rigorous.
findings.fix: Replace the characterisation with what the census supports: 'Interplanetary' returns 22 hits in (B): Maxwell quotations about the aether, the JPL probe-navigation and 1961 Venus-radar material on the speed of light, and single mentions of comets, the Mercury perihelion residual and the Pioneer anomaly - where interplanetary dust is raised and dismissed as a cause of the anomaly. None is an argument from zodiacal-cloud or Kuiper-belt structure. Drop 'None about dust' from the docstring.

findings.problem: The entry will fail the enforced suite. tests/test_provenance.py:190-193 fires on every full-depth argument with passage=None and requires the untraceable text to contain the literal string 'not that none exists' - the house formulation conceding that untraced means we did not find a source, not that none exists. C08, E06 and the E17 original all carry it; E10 does not. README calls tests/run.sh blocking, not advisory, so wiring batch 9 into deep.py turns the suite red. The substance of the concession is present ('That is a statement about those four texts and the OCR routes used to read them, and about nothing else'), so this is a missing clause rather than a missing idea.
findings.fix: Add the house sentence to the closing paragraph of `untraceable`, e.g. 'Untraceable here means we did not find a source, not that none exists: the four texts above and the searches described are the whole of what was read.'

findings.problem: Misattributed quotation. The text reads: each component 'is allowed to have a plane of symmetry that is different from the Ecliptic' (San et al., A&A 666:A107, 2022). That sentence is not in the 2022 ZodiPy paper; it is in Cosmoglobe DR2 III, arXiv:2408.11004 (2024), which this entry already cites two lines earlier. The 2022 paper's wording is 'each component is allowed to have some inclination i and ascending node Omega, with respect to the ecliptic.' The neighbouring San-attributed claim is fine - 'All IPD components, except the Earth-trailing feature, are distributed symmetrically around the Sun with respect to the ecliptic plane' is verbatim in the 2022 paper - which makes the error easy to miss and easy to fix.
findings.fix: Re-point the quotation to Cosmoglobe DR2 III (arXiv:2408.11004, 2024), or quote the 2022 paper's own wording instead.

findings.field: refutation, section 4 (scripts/_b9_E10.py:265); also docstring line 137 and the source label at line 421
findings.problem: The Siraj, Chyba & Tremaine statistics are paired with the wrong semimajor-axis bins. The paper says: 'in the 80-200 AU or 80-400 AU bin the measurement of the mean plane is in 2.52 sigma and 2.74 sigma tension, respectively ... these levels of significance imply false alarm probabilities of 4% and 2%, respectively' (and the abstract's 96%/98% confidences match that order). Our sentence lists the bins as '80-400 au and 80-200 au, at 2.52 sigma and 2.74 sigma - false-alarm probabilities of 4% and 2%', which a reader takes positionally and which inverts the paper's assignment.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: 'a warp relative to the invariable plane at 80-200 au (2.52 sigma, false-alarm probability 4%) and 80-400 au (2.74 sigma, 2%)', and correct the docstring and the source label to match.

findings.field: refutation, section 6 (scripts/_b9_E10.py:281) and the source entry at lines 447-450
findings.problem: Version mismatch on a quotation. The quoted words - the octopole 'consistently remains anomalously aligned with the quadrupole in all the CMB maps studied' - are verbatim in arXiv:2405.03024v1, but the citation given is the published MNRAS 539:542, where the sentence was rewritten to 'The octopole mode is anomalously aligned with the quadrupole mode in all CMB maps analysed in this study.' The source label also carries the v1 title ('CMB low multipole alignments across data releases') against the published volume and page; the published title is 'across WMAP and Planck data releases'. This is recurring failure 3 - edition and version dating - on a quote a reader is invited to verify.
findings.fix: Either quote the published sentence and keep the MNRAS 539:542 citation, or keep the v1 wording and cite it as arXiv:2405.03024v1 (2024), noting that the published version rephrases.

findings.problem: The strongest sentence available in our own cited source is unused, and it is in the section the advocate block designates as load-bearing. Planck 2013 XIV states: 'we emphasize that the zodiacal emission is essentially symmetric about the ecliptic plane, while the anomalies exhibit anti-symmetries about the plane. Thus, standard zodiacal emission cannot be evoked to explain the anomalies. This is consistent with the conclusions of Dikarev et al. (2008),' and that the zodiacal correction spectra are 'orders of magnitude smaller' than the CMB spectrum. We report only that the correction is 'small compared with the CMB temperature power spectrum'. The symmetry argument is exactly what makes our closing paragraph - that the ecliptic alignment of the dust and the ecliptic alignment of the microwave sky are two unrelated facts - airtight rather than merely asserted, and it comes from the Planck team rather than from us.
findings.fix: Add the symmetry sentence and 'orders of magnitude smaller' to the paragraph, immediately before 'But notice what the item costs whoever plays it', keeping it adjacent to the Planck 2013 XIV citation as the preemptive requires.

findings.problem: Patel, Aluri & Ralston is cited selectively in a way the entry's own stated standard forbids. Our clause - 'while also finding no preferred alignment among the low multipoles l = 2-61 taken collectively' - is defensible on the paper's section 4.8 and Fig. 6. But the same paper's summary is that 'the multipoles, not just few but collectively, indicate an intrinsic anisotropy of the data sets', that the first 60 modes are 'intrinsically anisotropic at greater than 95 per cent confidence level across data releases', and its abstract closes 'It appears that the CMB is not as random as the cosmological principle predicts on large angular scales.' Using it as the balancing note, with only the deflationary half quoted, is the same compression toward one's preferred conclusion that this project documents in others - and the entry explicitly commits to representing the astronomy 'at the strength the astronomers state it, including where it is unresolved'.
findings.fix: Add the paper's own conclusion in its own words after the quoted clause, e.g. 'while the same authors conclude that the low multipoles are collectively anomalous at about 2 sigma across every release, and that the CMB "is not as random as the cosmological principle predicts on large angular scales" - which is why E01 carries this debate rather than closing it.'

findings.field: tldr (scripts/_b9_E10.py:182) and refutation section 1 (line 234); the claim is also relied on in advocate.preemptive (b)
findings.problem: 'Two independent fits to the same COBE/DIRBE data' overstates, and the preemptive explicitly makes this the load-bearing evidence ('the load is carried by the direction of the tilt ... on two independent fits'). Cosmoglobe DR2 III describes itself as re-deriving Kelsall's own parametric form - 'The parametric form of the ZL model is inspired by the original DIRBE model by Kelsall et al. (K98), but the specific best-fit parameter values are re-derived' - and it adds Planck HFI, WISE and Gaia data rather than using DIRBE alone. So the two fits share a model in which inclination and node are free parameters, and the second is a refit rather than an independent confirmation. A well-informed defender's reply is ready-made: both numbers come out of the same parameterisation, so agreement on a tilt is partly built in. The body already concedes the two disagree by more than their error bars; the TLDR concedes nothing.
findings.fix: Say 'two independent analyses of the DIRBE data, the second refitting Kelsall's parameterisation with Planck HFI, WISE and Gaia added', and in the TLDR drop 'independent' in favour of 'fitted twice, thirty years apart'. The claim that survives - that both fits put the surface off the ecliptic and toward the invariable plane - is unaffected.

findings.problem: Volk & Malhotra's distant-belt warp is presented as a live anomaly alongside Siraj et al., but the Siraj paper we cite in the same sentence reports the opposite for that bin: 'The data are consistent with the invariable plane in the 50 - 80 AU bin, as previous work has shown (Van Laerhoven et al. 2019; Matheson & Malhotra 2023)', and warns that the new warp's 'statistical significance ... could wane, as was the case for the warp reported by Volk & Malhotra (2017)'. Our text says only that V&M 'reported' it, which is literally true, but a reader takes the two results as mutually supporting when the later one supersedes the earlier. The docstring knows this ('That result has an erratum and a contested history'); the published prose does not say it.
findings.fix: Add one clause: 'Volk & Malhotra's 50-80 au warp has not held up - Siraj et al. find that bin consistent with the invariable plane, and note their own result could wane the same way as the sample grows.' This makes the 'we state live things as live' claim true rather than asserted.

findings.problem: The solar apex is defined two different ways four sentences apart. First: 'the direction of the Sun's motion relative to the local standard of rest, in Hercules near Vega at RA 18h28m, Dec +30' - which matches the cited Wikipedia source and the 13.4 km/s figure used later. Then: 'The solar apex is the Sun's motion relative to the average of the nearby stars.' Those are different quantities; the standard solar motion relative to nearby stars is about 19.5 km/s, not the ~13 km/s the paragraph goes on to use. The 48.3 deg arithmetic is unaffected, but the payoff paragraph of the section contradicts its own definition.
findings.fix: Use the LSR definition in both places, and keep 'two different reference materials' as the contrast (Local Interstellar Cloud at ~26 km/s versus the local standard of rest at ~13.4 km/s).

findings.problem: The 1970 L2 bound is softened in our favour. The cited source states that the observations left 'material around the L2 point could contribute at most 6% of the gegenschein's light'; we write 'a few per cent of the light' in both places. Six per cent is not a few, and the exact number is stronger rhetorically because it is a specific published bound rather than a vague one.
findings.fix: Write 'bounded any L2 contribution at 6% of the light' in both places.

findings.problem: 'fitting the emissivities ... across nine frequencies' misreports the Planck zodiacal paper. The nine frequencies from 30 to 857 GHz are Planck's full set as described in the abstract; the zodiacal analysis states 'This work uses data only at frequencies of 100 GHz and higher', i.e. the six HFI bands. Small, but it is a numeric claim contradicted by the methods section of the paper cited for it, and this project asserts every published number in its tests.
findings.fix: Change 'across nine frequencies' to 'across Planck's six HFI frequencies, 100 to 857 GHz'.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py:591 (E10 cluster note), reported up at scripts/_b9_E10.py:168-174
findings.problem: This is recurring failure 5, and the report-up route is the one batch 8 showed does not get applied. The cluster note - 'Solar-system material lies in the solar-system plane. That is what a solar system is.' - becomes `basis` in build.py:156 and renders twice in render.py: on the summary line beside the verdict chip and again as the collapsed summary of section 3, so it is read by people who never expand the entry. Directly beneath it, section 1 of the refutation is headed 'The plane is measured, and it is not ours' and states that 'there is no single "solar-system plane"'. The docstring diagnoses this precisely and correctly declines to write around it, but as written the page will publish the contradiction. The docstring's stated reason for not editing ('assign.py is not this file's to edit') applies to item 332's assignment, not to clusters.py, which README lists as the place a basis line is edited.
findings.fix: Apply the note edit on the cluster key before this entry ships, to something the refutation supports - e.g. 'Solar-system material lies near a family of planes set by the planets' secular perturbations. The ecliptic is one member of that family, and not the best fit to the dust.' Item 332's cluster assignment is a separate report and can stay reported.

findings.field: refutation, section 3 ("Be exact about what that does and does not prove...")
findings.problem: The sentence "this clause was never carried as a shape claim by anybody, in either direction" is an unscoped universal negative about the entire reception history, and it is contradicted by the entry's own passage block. Carpenter's Proof 50 adduces "established that it cannot be moved" as one of the "allusions which could not be made if the Earth were a globe", inside a proof whose stated conclusion is "that Earth is not a globe" — the gloss says so itself ("Carpenter's conclusion is a claim about shape... The immovability clause is one of three illustrations"). The list under review carries the same clause in a flat-earth proof list. So the clause has been carried as a shape claim by at least two parties, one of them the source quoted at the top of this entry. The trailing "in either direction" closes the only available escape reading. The regex ratchet does not catch "never carried", which is precisely the failure mode the batch-8 sweep predicted.
findings.fix: Replace with the claim the evidence supports: "the clause itself says nothing about shape, and the traditions that recited it weekly attached it to a word for the world that settles nothing about geometry — which is why Carpenter, who does put it to work against a globe, has to reach it through an argument from silence rather than from the sentence." That keeps the paragraph's force, removes the universal negative, and turns the Carpenter counterexample into support.

findings.field: clusters.py C01 record → rendered meta line and originator_work (reported in the docstring, not applied)
findings.problem: clusters.py credits C01 to originator="William Carpenter", originator_work="One Hundred Proofs (proof 50 onward)", and render.py emits "first published by William Carpenter" in the meta line directly above the entry. This treatment establishes, and I independently verified, that there is no "onward" (exactly 100 proofs, exactly one scriptural), that Proof 50 carries no chapter-and-verse citation for any of the four verses, and that Psalm 104:5's clause is not among the phrases he quotes. A reader who never expands the entry — the skim path — reads a first-publication attribution for four verse citations that the source does not contain. The docstring discloses this and says it was reported upward in `record_problems`, which is correct process for an agent that does not own clusters.py, but no `record_problems` key exists in ENTRY and no handoff file carries it, so the report has no artefact in the repo. This is the fifth appearance of the recorded-but-not-applied pattern named in review/curmudgeon.md.
findings.fix: Belongs to the parent, not to this file. Anchor on the cluster key, never on the originator= line (it is byte-identical across several clusters). Proposed shape: originator_work="One Hundred Proofs, proof 50", year="1885", plus note="Proof 50 carries the shared KJV clause unattributed; the four chapter-and-verse citations and Psalm 104:5 are not located in the Gutenberg text of the 5th edition (#55387)." If the parent prefers, the C02 route — withdraw the credit and record the citations as untraced — is also defensible, but it must not be left as it stands. findings.problem: The TLDR runs "None of the four is about shape either: the psalter recited in English parish churches since 1549 renders the flagship verse 'He hath made the round world so sure: that it cannot be moved'" — deploying Coverdale's "round world" as the headline evidence with none of the concession the body spends a full paragraph making. The body is scrupulous: orbis terrae means circle or disc as readily as globe, ARG-C05 refuses the same move on Hebrew chûg, "we do not get to use a translator's word as evidence in one cluster having refused it in another." The advocate block's own preemptive (a) says that concession "must not be cut for length; without it the strongest paragraph on the page becomes the most vulnerable." It was cut in the one field readers see first and may never expand — and the advocate's third move is a defender attacking exactly this as a double standard. This is the recurring TLDR-stronger-than-body failure, in its subtler form: not a wrong quantifier but a missing qualifier.
findings.fix: Recast so the TLDR states the narrow claim rather than implying the wide one: "None of the four says anything about shape: the psalter recited in English parish churches since 1549 pairs the very same clause with the words 'the round world' — which settles nothing about geometry in either direction, and that is the point. Carpenter's own book prints a clergyman making it and answers him in a bracket."

findings.problem: Item 410 is enlisted as a list item that "points the other way", quoted as Psalm 75:3, "The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved." The quotation stops at the colon. The verse continues "I bear up the pillars of it" — and the list item's own phrasing is "Psalm 75:3 pillars of Earth.", filed at C03, "Proof-texts on foundations and pillars". The list is citing that verse for stability, not for dissolution. Presenting it as a counter-pull requires cutting the half the item actually names, which is the compression move this project exists to object to. Job 9:6 (item 411) is a clean trigger and carries the section on its own. In the same sentence, "four hundred items away" overstates a countable quantity: 411−61 = 350 and 410−61 = 349.
findings.fix: Drop item 410 from both passages and let Job 9:6 carry it, or quote Psalm 75:3 whole and say plainly that the list files it for the pillars while the same verse dissolves the earth two clauses earlier — which is a sharper version of the same method finding. Change "four hundred items away" to "three hundred and fifty items away".

findings.problem: "the position Carpenter assigns to the other side is not one his own century's critics held" is an unsourced historical negative about an entire generation of critics, and it is probably false. Carpenter assigns to the other side the view that scripture's cosmological allusions are absurd and contrary to established fact — which is close to what Draper's History of the Conflict between Religion and Science (1874) and A. D. White's The Warfare of Science (1876) were in print arguing eleven and nine years before this pamphlet. The evidence the entry actually offers (Calvin, the psalter, a creationist astronomer) shows that the best answers to these verses come from inside the tradition; it does not show that no contemporary critic held the position Carpenter describes. The first half of the finding — that no astronomer is quoted saying it in Proof 50 — is sound and does not need the second half.
findings.fix: Cut the clause and keep the verified point: "No astronomer is quoted saying it anywhere in Proof 50, and the readings that actually answer these four verses come from Calvin, from the psalter recited every month in English parish churches, and today from a creationist astronomer writing for Answers in Genesis. Casting the dispute as faith against infidelity conceals that it is a dispute about how to read a poem, conducted almost entirely among people who believe the poem."

findings.problem: "'Established that it cannot be moved' is the King James wording shared by Psalm 93:1 ..., Psalm 96:10 ... and 1 Chronicles 16:30" — but the three parentheticals that immediately follow prove that no two of them share it: KJV has "stablished, that it cannot be moved" (93:1), "established that it shall not be moved" (96:10) and "stable, that it be not moved" (16:30). Carpenter's phrase matches none of the three verbatim; it is a hybrid. Worth noticing rather than smoothing over: "that it cannot be moved" is the exact Book of Common Prayer wording at both Psalm 93 v.2 and Psalm 96 v.10, which I verified on the Church of England site — so the phrase Carpenter quotes from memory looks like the liturgical clause blended with the KJV verb, and the liturgical clause is the one that comes attached to "the round world".
findings.fix: "Carpenter's phrase matches none of the three verbatim — the KJV reads 'stablished, that it cannot be moved' (93:1), 'established that it shall not be moved' (96:10) and 'stable, that it be not moved' (16:30). It is the clause they share in Hebrew, quoted from memory and without attribution; and 'that it cannot be moved' is word for word the Prayer Book psalter's wording of the same verses — the psalter that renders the subject 'the round world'."

findings.problem: The Mach bucket quotation is not the wording of the edition we cite, and our own sentence asserting it is not out of context is false. We print: 'Try to fix Newton's bucket and rotate the heaven of fixed stars and then prove the absence of centrifugal forces,' framed as Mach challenging the reader, followed by 'That is not a misquotation and it is not out of context.' In the printing our sources name (archive cu31924004010504, McCormack second English edition, Open Court 1902) the sentence is in the Appendix at p. 543 and reads: 'Can we fix Newton's bucket of water, rotate the fixed stars, and then prove the absence of centrifugal forces? The experiment is impossible, the idea is meaningless, for the two cases are not, in sense-perception, distinguishable from each other.' Searches of that full text for 'Try to fix Newton' and 'rotate the heaven' return zero hits, and our sources label points only at pp. 231-232, where the 'several leagues thick' remark is. It is a rhetorical question Mach answers in the next breath, not a dare he leaves open. On a page whose thesis is that quotations lose their qualifiers as they pass through movement compilations, publishing a secondary-literature variant is the single most exploitable line in the file.
findings.fix: Quote as printed and keep the following sentence, which helps us: 'Can we fix Newton's bucket of water, rotate the fixed stars, and then prove the absence of centrifugal forces? The experiment is impossible, the idea is meaningless, for the two cases are not, in sense-perception, distinguishable from each other' (Appendix, p. 543 of the McCormack second English edition). Add the Appendix page to the sources label alongside pp. 231-232, and delete 'That is not a misquotation and it is not out of context'; the accurate version is that the substance is Mach's and the sentence is quoted here as he wrote it.

findings.problem: The strongest defence in the file is rated 4 — 'must be answered in the body' — and is not answered in the body, as preemptive (b) itself says: 'THE ANGULAR-MOMENTUM REPLY NEEDS ONE MORE SENTENCE IN THE BODY.' The advocate block is stripped from the published corpus by build.py and guarded by a test ('advocate mode panel is INTERNAL - never rendered to the page'), so the reply reaches no reader. The objection — that in a relational theory you do not get to compute 'the angular momentum of the universe' in an outside frame and wave it at us — goes directly at the section the entry calls 'the centre of it', and a reader who thinks of it finds nothing.
findings.fix: Land preemptive (b) in the third section: the vanishing is a constraint on the matter itself, not an absolute-space quantity imported from outside, which is why Lynden-Bell, Katz and Bicak present it as a vindication of Mach rather than of Newton, and why Barbour reaches the same restriction from pure invariance under time-dependent rotations with no background at all — two independent relational routes to the same exclusion. Bondi & Samuel supply a third citation for it in a source already in our list: their Mach5 entry reads 'In EC it is claimed that the total angular momentum of a closed universe must vanish' (gr-qc/9607009).

The only companion document is a one-page corrigendum, Eur. J. Phys. 34 (2013) 817, DOI 10.1088/0143-0807/34/3/817 (Crossref gives the page range as 817-817), which is mentioned in the module docstring but appears nowhere in the eleven-item sources list, and which I could not obtain. This is the shape of the batch-8 'the Pacific sea floor' finding: a specific figure in a rendered field with no locatable origin.

The KERNEL does not need it: Popov's published Sun-Earth-Mars result plus Assis's bulge, pendulum and Coriolis derivations already carry the concession.

findings.problem: Galileo Was Wrong cites Assis's earlier book, and we answer the later one without saying so. The scan carries exactly two Assis references, a footnote and a bibliography entry, both reading 'A. Assis, Rational Mechanics, Apeiron Press, Montreal, Canada 1999' — OCR for Relational Mechanics, Apeiron 1999. Our sources cite the 2014 successor, Relational Mechanics and Implementation of Mach's Principle with Weber's Gravitational Force, with no year and no note that the source used the 1999 volume. That is recurring failure 3 in miniature, and it also costs us a strengthening: those two references are the documented path by which item 295, 'Relational mechanics fixed Earth', reaches this source, which the compression block currently leaves as an assumption.

findings.problem: The closed-universe antecedent is used in both directions on the same page. The gloss argues the condition was quoted and then dropped and that closure is not favoured, citing Planck's Omega_K = 0.0007 +/- 0.0019 with lensing and BAO. The refutation then makes that same conditional theorem 'the centre of it' and says the geocentric arrangement is 'precisely the configuration the theorem forbids' — which needs the antecedent to hold. A defender gets two free jabs: our own page supplies the defeater for our own centrepiece, and we quoted the dataset combination that suits us, when Planck's TT,TE,EE+lowE spectra alone prefer Omega_K < 0 and there is a visible 'Planck evidence for a closed universe' literature saying so.
findings.fix: State in the third section that the argument there is internal to the source's own citation — it does not require the universe to be closed, only that the source's chosen authority, on its own terms, excludes the source's model, and that if closure fails the source loses the citation altogether. Then add the Planck-alone caveat in our own voice next to the Omega_K number, the way the sixth section already does for the vorticity bound.
