findings.problem: Published prose asserts a uniqueness about Hall that his text refutes: "the one concentric-circle cosmology Hall sets out at length is Pythagoras's ten spheres turning about a central fire, in which the Earth is one of the ten and is not at the centre." I downloaded the same text (archive item the-secret-teachings-of-all-ages_202012, 314,505 words). The Pythagorean passage is real and correctly described. But it is not the only one, and the others run the defender's way: Hall sets out at length a Fludd-derived Qabbalistic scheme of concentric rings in which "D to E marks the surface of the earth and sea", "F to G marks the circle of the subterranean air" and "G is the region of the central fire of the element earth" — a concentric cosmos with the earth at its middle — and he relays the music-of-the-spheres scheme in which "the planets in their revolutions round the earth uttered certain sounds ... Saturn, the farthest planet ... the Moon, which is the nearest", plus the sphere of the fixed stars. A defender who opens the book we cite finds a geocentric concentric cosmology inside two paragraphs. This is a quantifier in published prose, which is the failure mode the last two sweeps flagged, and it is gratuitous: the sentence is an aside marked "Worth adding", so nothing downstream depends on it.
findings.fix: Drop the uniqueness. Replace with: "Worth adding, since the list wants concentric circles: the concentric-circle cosmologies Hall relays are pagan and Hermetic, not Christian-devotional — Pythagoras's ten spheres turning about a central fire, in which the Earth is one of the ten and is not at the centre, alongside the older scheme of planets revolving round a central earth. Neither is derived from church imagery, and no conclusion about the Earth's shape is drawn from church imagery in the text searched."

findings.problem: We cite Todorova as the strongest form of the argument, then omit the single sentence in her paper that states items 432 and 448 almost verbatim. I pulled the PDF (revistas.ucm.es .../download/73399/4564456555341/4564456602656). Section 4 reads: "The mandorla is frequently perceived as a symbol of cosmos, according to the interpretations of St. Maximus the Confessor on the cosmological dimensions of the Transfiguration of Christ. Its inner concentric circles are considered as an image of all spheres of the created Universe" (citing Evdokimov, The Art of the Icon, p. 305, and Pseudo-Dionysius's celestial hierarchy). We quote only the adjacent "Imago Dei / symbolic Imago Mundi" line and then write that she "is not available as a witness for the conclusion" and that "Her mandorla is a symbolic imago mundi — a way of picturing ... what is invisible to the eyes". A defender who has read the paper calls that selective quotation of our own cited scholar, and on a provenance site that is the most expensive kind of hit. It also leaves us with a weaker rebuttal than the one available: our answer is that the mandorla darkens inwards so it is not a picture of lights, when the decisive answer is that spheres of the created universe are the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic spheres — geocentric AND spherical-Earth — which is the concession section 5 already makes and routes to ARG-C07.
findings.fix: Put her sentence in the steelman's KERNEL: "Todorova reports the standing Byzantine reading directly — the mandorla 'is frequently perceived as a symbol of cosmos', and 'its inner concentric circles are considered as an image of all spheres of the created Universe'. That is item 432 and item 448, in a peer-reviewed journal, in the affirmative." Then answer it in why_it_doesnt_save_claim before the darkening argument: "Grant it in full. The spheres of the created universe in that sentence are the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic spheres, and that system is geocentric and spherical-Earth. Conceding it hands the specimen a cosmology it cannot spend in a flat-Earth list, and the geocentric half is already scored at ARG-C07."

findings.problem: A quotation is attributed to an institution that did not publish it. We write "in the description given by Westminster Abbey's catalogue entry for it, 'in his left he holds another small image of Earth. We know it to be Earth from the T inscribed on it'", and the sources list repeats "Westminster Abbey's catalogue entry". I fetched the cited URL: the quote is real and the URL is right, but the asset is on Google Arts & Culture and the partner supplying the text is Fundación Elkano (Getaria, Spain); the manuscript itself is British Library Add MS 28681, which our own sentence correctly names. "Westminster Abbey" appears only in the asset's title, "Psalter World Map from Westminster Abbey". So we have credited a cathedral's catalogue for a Spanish foundation's exhibit caption. This sentence is load-bearing — it is the evidence for the disc-and-orb doubling that the advocate's preemptive explicitly instructs future editors to protect — and it is exactly the citation defect this site is built to expose in other people. Same paragraph dates the leaf "about 1270"; the cited entry says "around 1265".
findings.fix: Re-attribute and downgrade the authority: "...and, in the caption Fundación Elkano supplies for it on Google Arts & Culture, 'in his left he holds another small image of Earth. We know it to be Earth from the T inscribed on it'." Change the sources label to "Psalter world map, British Library Add MS 28681, c. 1265 — Google Arts & Culture entry (partner: Fundación Elkano)", set the date in the body to "about 1265", and if the sentence is to carry weight, add the Wikipedia "Psalter world map" record or the BL catalogue alongside it.

findings.problem: Item 365 "Metonic precision." is traced to the 1881 almanac-tabulation paragraph on the ground that "the nineteen-year repeat is the Metonic cycle". It is not — it is the Saros. Rowbotham's own text (sacred-texts za29.htm, p. 153-154, fetched and read) says the repeats occur "in every cycle of between eighteen and nineteen years" and illustrates it with a train passing "every eighteenth day"; the "nineteenth and twentieth years" are table ROWS, i.e. an 18-year interval, and the chapter has already defined that interval as the Saros of 6,585 1/3 days. Dubay's 2018 post frames the same passage as "18 year cycles"; the FES wiki quotes Ball as "eighteen years, or nineteen years... 6585 1/3 days". The Metonic cycle is a lunisolar calendar cycle (235 synodic months to 19 tropical years), which is what the entry's own section five correctly analyses — a different quantity from the one in the source passage. "Metonic", "draconic" and "nineteen" return zero hits in the 1865 Gutenberg text (#69892) and "Metonic" returns zero in the 1881 chapter. This makes three downstream statements overclaims: "Every one of the four quantities the list names... is in this chapter" (which also contradicts gloss paragraph four, where the nineteen-year material is correctly said not to be in the 1865 text), "Rowbotham's chapter supplies every one of the four quantities", and the verdict_challenge's "a search for the four named quantities returned a documented lineage in one chapter". On a page whose product is provenance, this is the load-bearing claim of the whole entry.
findings.fix: Narrow the attribution to what the chapter contains: the node, the Saros and the apogee (the last being a quantity the list does not name). Say that the 1881 recipe recovers the SAROS by counting, not the Metonic cycle, and quote Rowbotham's "every cycle of between eighteen and nineteen years" as the proof. Then note that a Metonic reference does exist in the modern carrier already cited here — the Flat Earth Society wiki quotes T. G. Ferguson (Earth Review, September 1894) quoting Keith: "The cycle of the moon is said to have been discovered by Meton, an Athenian in B.C. 433" — and route item 365 there, or mark it untraced rather than guessed. Delete "Every one of the four quantities the list names... is in this chapter" and "supplies every one of the four quantities and none of the four assertions", replacing both with the count that survives.

findings.problem: "So this material did not reach the modern list through the Victorian proof-list at all: it stayed in Rowbotham's prose chapter for a century and was lifted back out of it directly." The premise is a correctly scoped keyword search ("Saros", "Metonic" and "node" are indeed absent from Carpenter PG #55387 — I re-ran it, zero hits each), but the conclusion is about an ARGUMENT, and the argument is in Carpenter. His numbered proof 66 reads: "It is often said that the predictions of eclipses prove astronomers to be right in their theories. But it is not seen that this proves too much. It is well known that Ptolemy predicted eclipses for six-hundred years, on the basis of a plane Earth, with as much accuracy as they are predicted by modern observers." That is the theory-independence claim this entry identifies as the one descending to Dubay and the FES wiki — including the Ptolemy/600-years detail that Rowbotham takes from Smith and that Dubay reproduces. So the Victorian numbered proof-list carries this material as its own numbered item, and a defender refutes our sentence with one click on a source we cite ourselves. The sentence also carries weight beyond this entry: it is offered as "a small but clean piece of evidence for the project's general finding" about distributors returning to originals.
findings.fix: Replace with what the search actually established: "The technical vocabulary did not travel by this route — the words 'Saros', 'Metonic' and 'node' are not located in the Project Gutenberg text of Carpenter's One Hundred Proofs (1885, ebook #55387). The argument did: Carpenter's proof 66 states the theory-independence claim in his own words, without the cycle names. (b) The prescribed sentence scoping Delta-T as one scalar function of time constrained by hundreds of independent records, not a per-eclipse free parameter, is absent from section eight — I searched the refutation for "scalar", "free parameter", "initial condition", "constants": none present. Cross-reference the Clairaut case explicitly as the demonstration: the perigee rate could not be fitted, came out wrong by a factor of two, and nearly killed the theory. Add to section eight: Delta-T is one scalar function of time, the accumulated phase of the Earth's rotation, constrained by hundreds of independent records and used unchanged across eclipses, occultations and transits — not a per-eclipse adjustment. Then correct docstring note 6 to describe what was actually done.

findings.field: refutation, section seven (line 155); repeated in docstring note 5 (line 68)
findings.problem: "And the residual error of the lunar theory in those predictions is stated as 'of the order of 1/40 second'." The quote is exact but the characterisation is not what EclipseWise says. In context the 1/40 second is the error introduced by THEIR truncation of ELP-2000/82 — "we neglected all periodic terms with coefficients smaller than 0.0005 arcsecond... the Moon's positions calculated in our program have a mean error (as compared to the full ELP theory) of about 0.0006 second of time in right ascension... The corresponding error in the calculated times of the phases of a solar eclipse is of the order of 1/40 second". It is an implementation error measured against the full theory, not the theory's residual against reality. This is the rubric's "claims about what a source says that the source doesn't say" in miniature, and it is the kind of misreading a defender uses to argue we quote sources we have not read carefully.

findings.field: refutation, section nine (line 159) against section four (line 149)
findings.problem: "The Saros cannot give the where: its third-of-a-day remainder throws the next one roughly 116 deg of longitude away, so placing the shadow requires the rotation rate of the body the shadow falls on." Our own section four has already told the reader the opposite half: "the ancients had to stack three Saroses into the exeligmos of 19,756 days to get the geography back". The exeligmos is purely empirical — it needs no rotation rate, no globe, nothing but the observation that three Saroses come out near a whole number of days — and it returns the eclipse to roughly the same region, as NASA says on the page we cite ("a Saros series returns to about the same geographic region every 3 saroses"). So cycles do give an approximate where, and a defender will quote our own paragraph back at us. The strong claim we can actually defend is about precision, and the rest of the section already makes it.
findings.fix: "The Saros gives the where only to within a third of the globe, and the ancients could only recover the region by stacking three of them into the exeligmos. What the modern canons publish is an umbral track — a central line in latitude and longitude on a specified reference ellipsoid, contact times to the second, the duration of totality at each point — decades ahead, and it is met. No stack of recurrences yields that; it is a statement about the shape of the surface intercepting the shadow and the rate at which it turns."

findings.problem: "Divide that window by the drift and a series survives 64 to 77 repeats". The quoted ecliptic limit, 15.39 deg to 18.59 deg, is a half-width — EclipseWise's body sentence is "If New Moon takes place within about 17 deg of a node" with that range as its footnote. A reader who divides as instructed gets 32 to 39, not 64 to 77; the figures only reproduce if the limit is doubled first. The entry's own docstring makes reproducibility a design goal, and this is the one step a reader cannot follow.
findings.fix: "A solar eclipse is possible while the New Moon falls within about 17 deg of a node on either side — 15.39 deg to 18.59 deg... — so the usable window is roughly 31 to 37 deg wide. Divide that by the drift and a series survives 64 to 77 repeats..."

findings.problem: "the size of that residual is an open measurement." The body and the cited paper are more precise than this, and in the other direction: Stephenson, Morrison & Hohenkerk measure the observed rate at +1.78 +/- 0.03 ms/cy against a tidal +2.3 +/- 0.1, so the residual's size is measured, and rather tightly. What is open is its ATTRIBUTION (post-glacial rebound, core-mantle coupling), the reality of the ~1500-year oscillation, and extrapolation beyond the data — which is exactly what the body says and what the sources say. TLDRs are read by people who never expand, and prior sweeps found the TLDR is systematically stronger than the body; here it is looser.
findings.fix: "...and what causes the residual is still open."

LONDON: JOHN MURRAY, ALBEMARLE STREET. 1858." It is numbered, dated and identifiable. findings.problem: "the Solar System - eleven orders of magnitude above the MOND scale" is wrong, and it appears twice. With a0 = 1.2e-10 m/s^2, the Earth's orbital acceleration is GM_sun/r^2 = 5.93e-3 m/s^2, a factor of 4.9e7 = 10^7.7, not 10^11. At Neptune it is 6.5e-6 m/s^2, only 4.7 orders above. Eleven orders is the ratio for the Earth's SURFACE gravity (9.81/1.2e-10 = 8.2e10), which is not what the sentence is about. This sits in the paragraph our own advocate block calls "the only paragraph here that touches the list's actual thesis", so it is the most quotable error in the entry.
findings.fix: Replace with a figure that survives checking: "about eight orders of magnitude above that scale at the Earth's orbit and still four above it at Neptune", or better, the physical statement - "the MOND scale is not reached until roughly 7,000 AU from the Sun" (r = sqrt(GM_sun/a0) = 1.05e15 m).

findings.problem: "MOND partisans answer it with an ordinary-looking hot dark component such as sterile neutrinos (Angus, Famaey & Zhao, MNRAS 371:138, 2006)" attaches a claim to a paper that does not make it. Analytical comparisons of three versions of MOND beyond spherical symmetry" is an analytic study of potential-density pairs and non-spherical lensing in MOND and TeVeS; its abstract contains no neutrinos and no dark component. The neutrino answer to the Bullet Cluster is Angus, Shan, Zhao & Famaey 2007 (ApJ 654:L13, 2 eV active neutrinos) and Angus 2009 (the 11 eV sterile neutrino). findings.fix: Keep Angus/Famaey/Zhao for the modified-gravity modelling of the Bullet, and cite the neutrino move to its own paper: "MOND partisans answer it with a hot dark component - 2 eV neutrinos in Angus, Shan, Zhao & Famaey, ApJ 654:L13 (2007), an 11 eV sterile neutrino in Angus, MNRAS 394:527 (2009)". Also correct the matching sentence in advocate.preemptive (line 166), which names Angus/Famaey/Zhao as the counter.

findings.problem: "the version that made gravitational waves travel at the speed of light was killed by GW170817" states the opposite of the cited paper. Boran, Desai, Kahya & Woodard falsify "dark matter emulators" - theories in which ordinary matter couples to a DIFFERENT metric from gravitational waves, so the two signals accrue different Shapiro delays. What GW170817 killed is the family in which gravitational waves and light do not follow the same metric; what survives is a theory with gravitational waves at c, which is exactly what our own source label for Skordis & Zlosnik says that theory provides (line 277-280). The sentence contradicts both the cited paper and our own bibliography.
findings.fix: "the versions in which gravitational waves and light do not travel on the same metric were killed by GW170817 (Boran, Desai, Kahya & Woodard, Phys. Rev. D 97:041501, 2018), and Skordis and Zlosnik then built a theory in which they do, which also reproduces the microwave-background spectrum".

(p. 505)", with the Laemmerzahl quote at p. 506, "convenient phantoms" at p. 564, and the ch. 1 epicycle argument at pp. 59-61 - or, if the printed folios genuinely run the other way, say so once in the locator and apply it to every page number in the entry rather than mixing the two conventions.

findings.problem: The TLDR is stronger than the body, in the specific way both prior sweeps flagged, and it drops a hedge - our own version of the offence this project documents. findings.problem: The source's only empirical claim in the section we quote goes unanswered. Two pages after the passage in the quote box, the book cites the Hipparcos analysis - "The local dynamical density comes out as p0 = 0.076 +/- 0.015 ... leaving no room for any disk shaped component of dark matter" (Creze et al., footnote 989) - and draws the inference: "If there is no Dark Matter in the disc, we can logically assume that there is no such matter in the cosmos at large" (2006 Vol. I, p. 506). The hedge rule points straight at that sentence: it is the one place the source moves from rhetoric to data, and it is the easiest thing in the section to answer, since halo models predict a small local disc density and a measurement of the disc constrains the disc, not the halo. Our refutation answers a stronger version of the argument (the radial acceleration relation) and never touches the version the source actually ran.
findings.fix: Add a short paragraph before or after section 2: quote the book's own inference, note that the local dynamical density is a measurement of the Milky Way's disc while the dark matter in question is a roughly spherical halo, and that flat rotation curves at 20 kpc are unaffected by the density in the solar neighbourhood - so "none in the disc, therefore none in the cosmos" does not follow even if the disc figure stands.

findings.problem: Quoted material is weighted inconsistently. The Laemmerzahl sentence is discounted partly because it "is not the authors' own sentence", while the Scarpa material - which in the 2013 scan is a long quotation from a magazine report about Scarpa, in reported speech ("warns Scarpa", "he says") - is treated as the book's own approving account, and the Discover line ("in every single galaxy ever studied ...") is treated as the book's statement of the residual. A defender will notice that quotation counts as the book's position when it helps us and not when it does not. The substantive half of our point - that the Laemmerzahl sentence levels the approaches on evidence rather than on ad-hocery - stands on its own.
findings.fix: Delete the "not the authors' own sentence" leg and keep the evidential one, or apply the same standard to Scarpa ("quoted at length and without objection").

findings.problem: The locator names the section as "'Dark' Problems for Modern Notions of Gravity", which is the title in the volume's contents list. findings.problem: "Philolaus (5th century BCE) put fire, not Earth, at the centre. The witness is Aristotle... in De caelo II.13" — Aristotle is not the witness for Philolaus. I searched the Stocks translation at classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/heavens.mb.txt: the string "Philolaus" occurs zero times in the whole work. The quoted sentence is preceded by "But the Italian philosophers known as Pythagoreans take the contrary view" — Aristotle attests the doctrine and ascribes it to the school, never to the man. This matters because the sentence introducing the list insists "the testimony for them is ancient rather than modern reconstruction", and a defender who opens De caelo finds no Philolaus in it.
findings.fix: Rewrite the bullet: "Philolaus (5th century BCE) put fire, not Earth, at the centre. Aristotle attests the doctrine in De caelo II.13, ascribing it to “the Italian philosophers known as Pythagoreans” — “At the centre, they say, is fire, and the earth is one of the stars” — and the ancient doxographers (Aetius II.7.7) attach the name Philolaus to it, as does this book's own roster at p. 62." That keeps the claim ancient rather than modern and stops the bullet overstating what Aristotle says.

findings.problem: The entry concedes in two prominent places that "geocentrism was the default of the ancient world" / "geocentrism was the ancient default" and lists Babylonian, Egyptian, Norse and Mesoamerican cosmologies under it — then section Fourth argues at length that those very cultures cannot be geocentric at all, because geocentrism is a term of art requiring a cosmic centre and planetary orbits. Section Fourth tries to retcon this ("Note what was conceded in the first section" — geostasis) but the opening sentence and the TLDR both say geocentrism. A defender reads the first line back to us as the concession that sinks section Fourth.
findings.fix: Change the opening of First to "Geostasis — a world that does not move — was the default of the ancient world", keeping "and the learned tradition from Aristotle through Ptolemy made a stationary central Earth its first premise" for the properly geocentric half. Make the same substitution in the TLDR: "the weaker version that is true — a motionless Earth was the ancient default".

findings.problem: "...the exact failure this review documents twice elsewhere in family D, where descriptive scholarship about religious symbolism is read as testimony about geography (ARG-D04, ARG-D06)." findings.problem: "...a shift of roughly one degree, about two solar diameters, over the monument's lifetime." The numbers are right but the interval is not. Working the stated formula with the standard obliquity polynomial: ε = 23.974° at 2500 BCE and 23.44° today gives azimuths 49.63° and 50.62° — a 1.0° shift over 4,500 years, i.e. construction to the present day. Over the monument's actual lifetime (c. 3000 to c. 1500 BCE) ε runs 24.02° to 23.87° and the azimuth moves 49.53° to 49.85°, about 0.3° — a third of the figure quoted. The paragraph advertises reproducibility, so it invites exactly this check.
findings.fix: Replace "over the monument's lifetime" with "between its construction and today". If the lifetime figure is wanted instead, use "about a third of a degree across the monument's own working life, and a full degree between then and now".

findings.problem: The defence is rated survives=4, which the rubric defines as "strong — must be answered in the body", and the preemptive concedes the answer is not there: "the text must answer it rather than leave it implied... should state in one sentence". findings.fix: Add one sentence to the end of Third (a): "The objection that universal agreement about fire being hot is also produced by shared perception concedes the point rather than answering it — shared perception is excellent evidence about the appearance and none at all about the mechanism behind it. Everyone agreeing that fire feels hot settles what fire feels like, not phlogiston versus oxidation; everyone agreeing that the sky turns settles that the sky appears to turn, which both models predict." WHAT THE SOURCE ACTUALLY SAYS. The reachable copy of Galileo Was Wrong is the seventh edition (2013), and the Machian argument sits in Chapter 9, pp. 145-149, under three section headings that attach the word "Geocentrism" to physicists' names: "Nightingale's Geocentrism", "Lynden-Bell's Geocentrism", "Barbour and Bertotti's Geocentrism". The passage quoted for the entry (53 words, in-copyright, under the cap) is the chapter's conclusion: "geocentrism has been established by the very physics that sought to dethrone it in 1905."

THE KERNEL, AND IT IS IN THE SOURCE'S OWN PARAGRAPH. On p. 146 the book quotes Lynden-Bell, Katz & Bicak's "general proof that the angular momentum of any closed universe is zero" and reads it as providing "the fixed and undisturbed cradle for the barycenter, the Earth". That theorem is the one result in the cited literature that most directly excludes a cosmos circulating once a day: rigid circulation of all distant matter carries an enormous total angular momentum with nothing to cancel it. The same reversal repeats with Barbour & Bertotti, whose best-matching dynamics admits only the zero-total-angular-momentum sector (SEP: in shape dynamics "the overall angular momentum of the universe must vanish"), and whose paraphrase in the book itself records them proceeding "by assuming a non-rotating universe". The more Machian the theory, the less room for a turning sky.

THE STEELMAN IS CONCEDED AT FULL STRENGTH, because there is real work here: Popov, Eur. J. Phys. 34:383 (2013), does the Sun-Earth-Mars system twice and reproduces the geostatic trajectories and Proxima's 0.76" parallax; Assis's Relational Mechanics derives the equatorial bulge and Foucault precession from galaxies turning about a stationary Earth and concludes to "a complete equivalence between ptolemaic and copernican world systems". The answer is that Assis grants the same to every frame - "any other frame of reference would be equally valid ... anyone or any arbitrary frame of reference can be considered really at rest", his worked example being a falling rock - so the result is about frames, not about the Earth; that Popov's model is Newtonian and turns on a stipulated pseudo-potential plus "the assumption that orbits of distant masses around the Earth are synchronized with the Sun's orbit"; and that Assis's own text records the gaps (light deflection, gravitational redshift) and the price (a non-expanding, tired-light cosmos).

GENUINELY OPEN, AND SAID SO (E01 discipline). Mach's principle is unfinished physics, not settled physics: Bondi & Samuel enumerate eleven inequivalent versions and GR satisfies some and violates others; the Lynden-Bell result is conditional on a closed universe (Planck: Omega_K = 0.0007 +/- 0.0019). The entry says this in the body rather than pretending the question is closed. It also states its own weakest evidence in its own voice: the Planck vorticity bound (sigma_V/H < 4.7e-11, 95% CI) is derived inside a perturbed relativistic cosmology, so the argument is not rested on it; the light-cylinder radius c/Omega = 4.11e12 m = 27.5 AU and the internal-reversal argument do not depend on the framework.

Advocate rated 4 (best defence: "you answered Assis with Barbour and Barbour with Assis"; the angular-momentum move is an absolute quantity smuggled into a relational theory; the Planck bound is circular), with four concrete preemptive text changes. Straw man identified: the bracketed "[e.g., the universe]" / "[e.g., the Earth]" insertions and the "Geocentrism" section headings attribute a position on the Earth's motion to named researchers whose papers are about Mach's principle. Living people (Assis, Barbour, Bicak) are described only by what they wrote, never by imputed belief.

The headline is a source reversal, the A05 shape a second time in a different lineage. I downloaded both reachable Galileo Was Wrong plain-text scans whole (archive.org items GallileoWasWrong, 462k words, and …Bennett4276) and searched them locally rather than through a truncating fetch. Volume I, chapter 1, printed p. 62 opens the historical survey by describing ancient cosmology as a controversy "that stretches as far back as written records take us" and names an ancient heliocentric side; footnote 133 on the same spread adds Hicetas, Heraclides and Ecphantus as holding "that the Earth rotates in a non-moving heavens"; Appendix 9 footnote 1565 reproduces Dreyer's translation of Archimedes on Aristarchus. Four list items assert a universal their own cited authority denies. drift_type = reversed.

Hedge rule, both clauses. The refutation answers the source's real position — antiquity was divided, and the geocentric majority held its view on evidence — rather than the fragment: the majority is conceded in the first sentence, the evidence-driven reading is credited as the kernel (Aristotle nominated stellar parallax as the falsifier, which is why the kernel dies at Bessel 1838 and Gaia DR3), and the weight falls on what a consensus generated by a shared appearance can be worth. The weak, true reading ("near-universal default") is granted explicitly and then defeated twice: shared-appearance agreement is one observation repeated, not many witnesses; and the same consensus is just as firm about a spherical Earth, which a half-flat-earth list cannot spend selectively. Then the gap is published as a finding in the compression block, including that the source's actual appeal to antiquity (Vol. I p. 130, quoting Wolfgang Smith 2003) is a rhetorical question offered as grounds to reopen an inquiry.

Two pieces of original ground beyond the reversal. (1) "Cultures" cannot do the work: geocentrism is a term of art from Greek mathematical astronomy, so cosmologies with no cosmic centre and no planetary orbits — Nut and Geb, the Enūma Eliš, the world-tree — can neither affirm nor deny it; counting them recruits witnesses who left no testimony, which is the same failure the review already documents at D04 and D06. The concession in section one is scoped to geostasis, and the entry says so explicitly so the two sections do not read as contradicting each other. (2) The ancient world splits cleanly — the flat cosmologies are not geocentric in the technical sense, the geocentric ones are spherical-Earth — so no ancient culture supplies both halves of this list.

Item 367 ("Ancient stone calendars geocentric") is answered on its merits although its material is not located in either scan searched: horizon alignments are topocentric and predicted identically by both models (ARG-A22 cut in stone); the builders were preliterate and no statement of their cosmology survives; Atkinson's "Moonshine on Stonehenge" (Antiquity 40, 1966, 212–216) is the cautionary case for reading cosmology off alignments, and Historic England's own research page warns that archaeoastronomy is "prone to misinterpretation and speculation". Added a reproducible calculation: obliquity 23.97° at 2500 BCE against 23.44° today moves midsummer sunrise azimuth at Stonehenge's latitude from ~49.6° to ~50.6°, about two solar diameters — and the entry says plainly that a geocentrist can redescribe that as a slow tilt of the sky at no kinematic cost, so the monument confirms nothing either way.
